bull.b: Recurring service revenue growth supports durable earnings visibility because it is tied to the expanding base of wireless and broadband subscriptions. Continued postpaid momentum and higher ARPA can strengthen revenue quality while supporting reinvestment in network capacity and customer acquisition.

A leading customer-satisfaction position can reinforce retention, acquisition, and share gains over multiple quarters. Combined with repeated third-party network awards, this indicates a competitive service proposition that may support customer lifetime value and reduce reliance on aggressive pricing.

Strong operating and free cash flow provide internal funding for network investment, spectrum opportunities, debt service, and shareholder returns. Cash-backed earnings improve financial resilience and give management more flexibility to pursue growth while maintaining disciplined capital allocation.

bear.b: Elevated leverage reduces financial flexibility because a larger share of future cash generation may be needed for debt-related obligations. Declining equity alongside high debt leaves less balance-sheet capacity to absorb weaker operating conditions or fund major spectrum investments.

Prepaid declines can weigh on subscriber scale and revenue diversification even when migration to postpaid benefits customer mix. Sustained weakness would make growth more dependent on postpaid additions and could pressure the contribution from a historically important service segment.

Higher customer out-of-pocket device costs may make upgrades and new activations less accessible, particularly for price-sensitive users. Lower subsidies protect economics but could slow equipment demand, complicate customer acquisition, and increase pressure on service growth if adoption weakens.
